bug_description.original: Heap-buffer-overflow in mrbgems/mruby-compiler/core/codegen.c: the dispatch (and dispatch_linked) code performs a 1-byte out-of-bounds read from a heap buffer during bytecode generation/dispatch. A crafted input can trigger this OOB read, leading to crashes, undefined behavior or potential information disclosure.
bug_description.normalized: A crafted Ruby source file can make mruby generate nested rescue bytecode with `genjmp2()` using an extended register operand (`a > 0xff`). In that `OP_EXT1` path, the vulnerable code stores the raw previous placeholder position with `gen_S(s, pc)` instead of encoding the jump destination with `gen_jmpdst()`. Later `dispatch_linked()` interprets that malformed 16-bit field as another relative linked-jump position, so `dispatch()` follows it outside `s->iseq` and performs a heap-buffer-overflow read.

source.description: The staged plain-text PoC is parsed into the AST `p->tree`. That AST shape is the first project-side materialization of attacker input that later drives the vulnerable rescue-code generation path.
source.value_from: The saved 26226-byte PoC starts with `#` (0x23), so `mrb_load_detect_file_cxt()` routes it through the Ruby source parser instead of the `RITE` bytecode loader. The exact witness also contains 1776 textual `rescue` tokens, and `mrb_parser_parse()` materializes that rescue-heavy structure into `p->tree` here.

sink.description: A later `dispatch()` iteration reads the next 16-bit jump-link field from an out-of-range `pos0`, so `PEEK_S` dereferences past the allocated bytecode buffer `s->iseq`. Stage 01 ASan reports the crash here as a 1-byte heap-buffer-overflow read.

root_cause.description: In the `a > 0xff` (`OP_EXT1`) branch, `genjmp2()` writes the raw 16-bit `pc` value into the jump-link field instead of calling `gen_jmpdst(s, pc)`. That violates the link-format contract later assumed by `dispatch()` and `dispatch_linked()`.

parser_admitted.code: if (bufsize < sizeof(leading.h) || memcmp(leading.h.binary_ident, RITE_BINARY_IDENT, sizeof(leading.h.binary_ident)) != 0 || memchr(leading.b, '\0', bufsize) == NULL) {
parser_admitted.description: The staged witness begins with `#` and is not a `RITE` bytecode file, so this predicate takes the Ruby-source path rather than the bytecode loader.

admitted_location.code: return mrb_load_exec(mrb, mrb_parse_file_continue(mrb, fp, leading.b, bufsize, c), c);

tainted_value_origin.code: tmp = genjmp2(s, OP_JMPIF, cursp(), pos2, val);
tainted_value_origin.description: The parsed rescue nesting first becomes the exact vulnerable operands here: the current register index `cursp()` and the linked-jump head `pos2` are handed to `genjmp2()`.

coarse_trace.summary: Recognizes the staged file as Ruby source text rather than `RITE` bytecode and routes it into the source parser.
Parses the staged source file into an AST whose repeated `rescue` structure is attacker-controlled.
Compiles nested `NODE_RESCUE` handlers and emits linked `JMPIF` placeholders whose register operand grows past 255.
The `OP_EXT1` jump-emission path stores malformed link metadata by writing raw `pc` bits into the jump field.
Later jump patching treats the malformed field as a linked placeholder and drives `dispatch()` into an out-of-bounds read from `s->iseq`.

fine_trace.note: Consumes the staged plain-text Ruby file and materializes `p->tree`. The exact witness starts with `#` and contains 1776 `rescue` tokens, so the attacker controls a rescue-heavy AST shape.
After syntax admission, mruby starts bytecode generation over the attacker-derived AST instead of rejecting the file.

Each nested `NODE_RESCUE` handler captures the exception and increments `s->sp`. The witness AST recurses through this block many times, so the live register index grows beyond 255 before the crashing jump emission.

fine_trace.code:
tmp = genjmp2(s, OP_JMPIF, cursp(), pos2, val);
pos2 = tmp;
fine_trace.note: The rescue matcher emits a linked `JMPIF` placeholder using the current register index as operand `a`; the returned slot position becomes the new jump-chain head `pos2`.
Because the attacker-driven nesting pushed `a` above one byte, `genjmp2()` selects the `OP_EXT1` encoding path for this jump.

The `OP_EXT1` branch writes raw 16-bit `pc` bits into the jump-link field instead of `gen_jmpdst(s, pc)`'s relative-link encoding or zero sentinel, leaving malformed placeholder metadata in `s->iseq`.
After emitting the rescue-clause jumps, codegen asks `dispatch_linked()` to patch the linked placeholder chain whose head is `pos2`, including the slot corrupted at step 5.
The first `dispatch()` invocation decodes the corrupted 16-bit field at `pos0` as a signed linked-placeholder delta `newpos`.
Because `newpos` came from raw placeholder bits rather than a real relative link, the computed next position is bogus and can leave the valid 2-byte jump-field region inside `s->iseq`.
The patcher loop trusts the nonzero returned `pos` and immediately re-enters `dispatch()` with it; there is no check that the next `pos0` still points inside the allocated bytecode buffer.

On this later `dispatch()` iteration, `pos0` is outside the allocated `s->iseq` buffer, so `PEEK_S` reads past the heap object. Stage 01 ASan reports the crash here as a 1-byte heap-buffer-overflow read 756 bytes beyond the 16384-byte allocation.

format.name: mruby source file
format.contract: The exact saved 26226-byte PoC is a plain-text Ruby script, not a `RITE` bytecode file: it begins with `#` (0x23), so `mrb_load_detect_file_cxt()` routes it through `mrb_parse_file_continue()`. In this witness, the script contains 1776 textual `rescue` tokens, producing a rescue-heavy AST that drives `codegen()` into `genjmp2()` with `cursp() > 0xff`, takes the `OP_EXT1` branch, and later triggers the malformed linked-jump read in `dispatch()`.
